concepts.label: Life in Hot Springs: Where Cells May Have Begun
concepts.cardText: It is widely accepted in the scientific community that life originated in water, and some researchers believe it may have begun in small water pools with changing conditions rather than in the oceans. Hot springs are examples: the Puga Valley hot springs in Ladakh stay near the boiling point of water even in a cold climate, conditions that seem similar to the early Earth about 3.5 billion years ago. Their organisms are mostly heat-loving unicellular bacteria called thermophiles. Calcium carbonate formed quickly around the springs; these deposits may have protected early organic molecules from radiation and extreme conditions and may have helped form the first protective membrane, the barrier that defines a cell.

concepts.label: The Cell as the Basic Unit of Life
concepts.cardText: All living organisms are made up of cells, and the cell represents the basic level at which life exists. Some organisms, such as bacteria or yeast, consist of only one cell (unicellular), while plants, fish, birds or humans are made of millions of cells (multicellular) that work together. A group of similar cells performing similar functions forms tissues, different tissues form an organ, and several organs working together form an organ system. Even then the cell remains the fundamental unit of structure and function in all living organisms.

concepts.label: Limit of Resolution and How Cells Are Studied
concepts.cardText: When viewed from about 25 cm, the near point of the human eye, two points separated by about 0.1 mm can be seen as distinct; otherwise they appear as a single point. This is the limit of resolution of the human eye, 0.1 mm. A cell is usually too small to be seen by the unaided eye, so cell biologists use a convex lens or a combination of lenses, an objective lens and an eyepiece, to magnify objects. Robert Hooke was the first person to observe a cell, in 1665, using a self-designed microscope of about 200-300X magnification; examining a thin slice of cork, he saw small box-like compartments and named them cells.

concepts.label: The Light Microscope and Estimating Cell Size
concepts.cardText: School laboratories use light microscopes with different objective lenses, such as 10X and 40X, for better magnification and resolution under visible light. To estimate the size of a cell (Activity 2.1), measure the diameter of the circular field of view using a ruler under the microscope and convert it to micrometres (1 mm = 1000 micrometres), then count the number of onion peel cells along the diameter. The estimated size of a cell is the diameter of the visible field in micrometres divided by the number of cells along the diameter: for a 5 mm field with 25 cells, 5000 micrometres divided by 25 gives 200 micrometres. The total magnification depends on the magnifying power of the eyepiece and the objective lens, so with 10X for both it is 100X, and a 200 micrometre cell appears 100 times larger.

concepts.label: Improving Microscopes: Resolution, Contrast and Electron Microscopes
concepts.cardText: A microscope allows us to see very small structures clearly and is an essential tool for studying cell structure. Over the years scientists have improved the microscope by improving three main features: resolution (the measure of clarity), contrast (the difference in brightness between various parts of an object) and magnification. Electron microscopes use a beam of electrons instead of light to produce highly magnified images, allowing cell structure to be seen at the nanometre scale (a nanometre is one-billionth of a metre) with remarkable clarity. An example is the picture of the lower surface of a Colocasia leaf taken with a scanning electron microscope.

concepts.label: The Cell Membrane
concepts.cardText: For cells to function as units they must interact with one another and with their surroundings, and these interactions occur at the cell boundary, where substances move between the cells and their external environment. Even single-celled organisms exchange materials and respond to their environment through the cell membrane. The cell membrane, also called the plasma membrane, is a thin boundary that surrounds a cell and protects its contents, and it defines the individuality of a cell. It is selectively permeable, which means it allows some substances to pass through it while blocking others.

concepts.label: Diffusion and Osmosis: The Potato Experiment
concepts.cardText: In Activity 2.2 two roughly equal potato pieces are weighed, one placed in plain water and one in 20 per cent salt or sugar solution. The piece in plain water swells and gains weight, while the piece in the solution shrinks and loses weight. This happens because the cell membrane allows water to move in and out of the cell but not the sugar or salt molecules. Water moves from an area with more water and less solute (a dilute solution) to an area with less water and more solute (a concentrated solution) until the concentrations in the two areas become equal. This movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane is osmosis. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration, which occurs even without a membrane, because particles of matter intermix due to a concentration gradient; osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. In plants, water from the soil enters root cells by osmosis.

concepts.label: Isotonic, Hypotonic and Hypertonic Solutions
concepts.cardText: A cell kept in salt or sugar solutions of different concentrations behaves differently according to the solute concentration outside compared with inside. When the solute concentration of the extracellular medium equals that of the intracellular medium, the solution is isotonic. When the extracellular solute concentration is lower than the intracellular, the solution is hypotonic. When the extracellular solute concentration is higher than the intracellular, the solution is hypertonic.

concepts.label: Structure of the Cell Membrane: The Fluid-Mosaic Model
concepts.cardText: The cell membrane is extremely thin, about 7 to 10 nanometres thick, and is made up of lipids (fats) and proteins. The fluid-mosaic model explains its structure: the membrane has a lipid bilayer, two layers of special fat molecules with water-attracting heads outwards and water-repelling tails inwards, with proteins embedded in them. The molecules can move sideways, flip and rotate within the membrane, so it is fluid. Proteins in the membrane act like gatekeepers in helping substances pass through. Since the molecules are arranged like tiles in a mosaic, it is called the mosaic model.

concepts.label: The Cell Wall
concepts.cardText: All living cells communicate with their surroundings through the cell membrane, but cells of plants, fungi and bacteria have an additional layer around the cell membrane, the cell wall. Plants cannot move from place to place, so they need a rigid structure to withstand environmental stresses like wind and rain; the cell wall also helps leaves and flowers remain firm and keeps plants upright. Although rigid, the cell wall is permeable, so water and some dissolved minerals pass through it, which with the membrane's selective permeability helps roots absorb water and nutrients. When a Rhoeo leaf or onion peel is put in concentrated sugar solution, the plant cells lose water by osmosis but do not shrink in size because the rigid cell wall maintains their shape; the inner content shrinks as the membrane pulls away from the wall. Animal cells such as cheek cells have no cell wall, so they lose water and shrink, and can easily change shape, which supports the movement of animal tissues. The plant cell wall is primarily made of cellulose, a carbohydrate of many glucose units, which in our diet acts as roughage; fungi and bacteria also have a cell wall.

concepts.label: Parts of the Cell: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
concepts.cardText: Most cells have three basic parts: a selectively permeable plasma membrane, a semi-fluid jelly-like cytoplasm, and a prominent nucleus. In addition to the nucleus, the cytoplasm contains sub-cellular components called organelles, most of which are visible only with an electron microscope. A bacterial cell lacks a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (organelles surrounded by their own membranes); such cells are prokaryotic (pro means primitive, karyon means nucleus), and most of their cellular activities take place directly in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotic DNA is present as a single circular molecule associated with specific proteins, in a region called the nucleoid. Plant and animal cells have a well-defined nucleus and several membrane-bound organelles; they are eukaryotic (eu means true). In eukaryotic cells a network of fine fibres forms the cytoskeleton, which provides structural support, maintains cell shape and enables cell movement and internal transport. The cytoplasm may also store starch or crystals of calcium oxalate or silica, known as cell inclusions.

concepts.label: Nucleus: House of Coded Instructions
concepts.cardText: The nucleus has a double-layered covering called the nuclear membrane with pores that allow transfer of material between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The nucleolus is the dense round body in the nucleus where ribosomal subunits are synthesised; they exit to the cytoplasm and assemble into ribosomes. The nucleus contains chromosomes, visible as rod-shaped structures only when the cell is about to divide. Chromosomes carry information for inheritance of characters from parents to the next generation in the form of DNA, and are composed of DNA and specific proteins. DNA molecules contain the genetic information, and the functional segments of DNA are called genes. In a non-dividing cell the DNA is part of chromatin material, an entangled mass of thread-like structures, which is organised into chromosomes when the cell is about to divide. Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus, giving more space for haemoglobin to carry oxygen, but they cannot repair or divide and survive only about 120 days.

concepts.label: Ribosomes and the Endoplasmic Reticulum
concepts.cardText: Ribosomes are tiny structures, present freely in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, and are the sites of protein synthesis. The Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) is a large organelle that spreads like a network within the cytoplasm and is continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. It plays a key role in the synthesis and transport of proteins, fats (lipids) and some hormones in some specialised cells, and its structure varies with its function. The Rough ER (RER) looks rough under an electron microscope because ribosomes are attached to its surface, and is mainly involved in protein synthesis and secretion, as in pancreatic gland cells. The Smooth ER (SER) has no ribosomes on its surface, looks smooth, and is involved in the synthesis and storage of fats and hormones.

concepts.label: Golgi Apparatus and Lysosomes
concepts.cardText: The Golgi apparatus is made of stacks of flattened, sac-like structures and is functionally linked to the ER, the cell membrane and other organelles. It acts like the cell's post office: it modifies, sorts and packages proteins and/or lipids into vesicles for transport, secretion or lysosome formation. Camillo Golgi first observed it in 1898 in the nerve cells of a barn owl; early microscopes could not resolve it clearly and many doubted its existence, but electron microscope observations confirmed it decades later. Cells produce waste and damaged, worn-out organelles, and lysosomes, single membrane-bound sacs filled with enzymes, break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged parts, keeping the cell clean and healthy; the breakdown products are released into the cytoplasm and may be reused. Sperm cells contain lysosomal enzymes that help break down the outer layer of the egg during fertilisation.

concepts.label: Mitochondria: The Powerhouse of the Cell
concepts.cardText: Mitochondria are often called the powerhouses of the cell because they supply the energy needed for most cellular activities. Each mitochondrion is surrounded by two membranes: the outer membrane is smooth and porous, and the inner membrane is folded into finger-like projections called cristae, which increase the surface area for chemical reactions and facilitate energy production. In mitochondria glucose and other molecules are broken down to release energy during cellular respiration, and the energy is stored in Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), which acts as the energy currency and is used for most cellular activities.

concepts.label: How Cells Grow and Divide
concepts.cardText: When a cut on the skin heals or lost hair grows back, it is because cells in our body can grow and divide to replace old, dead or damaged cells. Growth of the body is not just because cells get bigger: cells can grow only up to a certain size, so growth happens because cells divide to form new cells. The cells of a growing onion root tip divide continuously, which is why they show different structures corresponding to different stages of cell division. Every day an estimated hundreds of billions of cells in our body, almost 1 per cent of the total, are replaced. Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells divide, but eukaryotic cells divide in a more controlled and orderly way by the cell cycle. Cell division is the process by which new cells are formed from pre-existing cells; it allows organisms to grow, repair damaged tissues and reproduce, and skin cells divide continuously to replace cells lost regularly. There are two major types, mitosis and meiosis: mitosis is important for normal growth, repair, maintenance and asexual reproduction, while meiosis is important for sexual reproduction and creates genetic diversity.

concepts.label: Meiosis and Errors in Cell Division
concepts.cardText: Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces gametes and occurs only in the cells of reproductive organs. Gametes produced for sexual reproduction create variations and diversity among living organisms, so children resemble their parents but are not exactly the same. In animals meiosis occurs only in the testes of males to produce sperm and the ovaries of females to produce eggs; in plants it occurs in anthers to form pollen grains and in ovaries to produce egg cells. In meiosis the parent cell divides twice, one after the other, to form four daughter cells. In the first division the cells divide into two daughter cells and the chromosome number in each is reduced to half; the second division is similar to mitosis, so each daughter cell divides into two, forming four cells with half the number of chromosomes. During fertilisation, when gametes from two individuals combine, the original chromosome number is restored. Errors in mitosis lead to uncontrolled cell divisions, tumours and abnormal numbers of chromosomes in body cells, while errors in meiosis may cause genetic disorders, early pregnancy loss or reduced fertility.

concepts.label: Cell Culture and Totipotency
concepts.cardText: Scientists have developed methods to grow plant and animal cells outside the body in special conditions, called cell culture. Cells taken from an organism are placed in a nutrient-rich medium that lets them grow and multiply, with the right temperature, acidic or alkaline conditions and moisture kept under sterile conditions. Cell culture is crucial for studying how cells work and for producing biochemicals, food, medicines and vaccines. In 1902 the Austrian botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt proposed that any living plant cell, even a fully mature one, can develop into a complete plant given suitable nutrients and favourable conditions; this special ability of plant cells is called totipotency, and it laid the foundation for Plant Tissue Culture Technology.

concepts.label: Cell Theory
concepts.cardText: All organisms are made up of cells. In 1838 the German botanist Matthias Schleiden reported that all plants are made up of cells, and in 1839 the German zoologist Theodor Schwann found that all animals are also made up of cells. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow further expanded the Cell Theory by stating that new cells are formed only from pre-existing cells. According to the classical Cell Theory, all living organisms are made up of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living beings, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. This unifies all biology, from bacteria to humans, and explains life's continuity through cell division.

concepts.label: Life Span of Cells, Contact Inhibition and Cancer
concepts.cardText: Cells grow and divide in a controlled way, stay in the right place, carry out their functions and eventually die when no longer needed, and dead cells are replaced by new cells doing the same function; every cell has a definite life span. In many animal cells, division usually stops when cells come in contact with neighbouring cells, called contact inhibition. Cancer cells lose this control and keep dividing uncontrollably, leading to tumours, which may be benign or malignant; cancerous tumours can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body to form new tumours. Plant cells, because of their rigid cell walls, do not show contact inhibition and follow a different pattern of growth. Programmed Cell Death (PCD) is a genetically regulated and organised process of selective cell destruction that is essential for normal development, cellular quality control and immune function; for example, it helps form fingers in an embryo by eliminating cells between the digits.
